sentences.text: Morrosaurus antarcticus was a herbivorous dinosaur that lived in Antarctica during the late Cretaceous. The single known specimen is estimated to be between 4.5 and 5 meters in length, though other sources describe it as a medium-sized animal.
A partial skeleton of a euornithopod was discovered in Antarctica in 2002 by paleontologist Fernando Novas.
The species Morrosaurus antarcticus was named and described in 2016 by a team including Sebastian Rozadilla and Fernando Novas, although some records state the description occurred in 2015.
The genus name Morrosaurus refers to the fossil site of El Morro on James Ross Island, while the species name refers to Antarctica.

The holotype specimen MACN Pv 197 was found in the Snow Hill Island Formation at Cape Lambe and dates to the Maastrichtian age. The holotype specimen MACN Pv 197 was found in a layer of the Snow Hill Island Formation at Cabo Lambe, deposited in the López de Bertodano Formation.
The known remains consist of a right hind leg, including parts of the femur, tibia, foot, and the first joint of the third toe.

Members of the Elasmaria group, including Morrosaurus, show adaptations for a high-speed running lifestyle indicated by a narrow foot with a thin fourth metatarsal. Members of this group are distinguished by an adaptation to a running lifestyle, reflected by a narrow foot with a thin fourth metatarsal indicating high running speed.
The interrupted rapid growth strategy of Morrosaurus was likely an adaptation to the varying resource availability in Antarctica.
Morrosaurus is classified within Iguanodontia as a basal member of Euiguanodontia. Morrosaurus was placed in the group Iguanodontia as a basal member of Euiguanodontia.

Morrosaurus belongs to the clade Elasmaria, which includes ornithopods from Patagonia and Antarctica such as Trinisaura and Gasparinisaura. It forms a clade with other Patagonian and Antarctic ornithopods, particularly Trinisaura, Gasparinisaura, Anabisetia, Notohypsilophodon, Talenkauen, and Macrogryphosaurus, in a grouping called Elasmaria.
The close relationship between Antarctic Morrosaurus and South American elasmarians demonstrates faunal links between these continents.

Morrosaurus lived during the Maastrichtian age of the late Cretaceous period. It lived during the late Cretaceous period, 70 to 66 million years ago in the Maastrichtian, in the area of modern Antarctica. The time range is the Maastrichtian, from 72.2 to 66 million years ago.

It is debated whether Morrosaurus possessed the specific running adaptations of the Elasmaria clade due to the fragmentary nature of the fossil remains. It cannot be determined whether Morrosaurus itself possessed these characteristics due to its limited remains.
